Table 3.4 below summarizes the projected 2026 vessel activity at the Port of Tampa with operational parameters to inform potential expansion opportunities at the CO₂ offloading hub. Key metrics include main engine specifications, fuel consumption expectations, voyage durations, and estimated annual visit factors for calculating onboard carbon capture potential and transfer infrastructure requirements. The data reflects industry-standard propulsion systems for vessel classes frequenting the port, paired with fuel consumption quantities calibrated to typical ships sizes and voyage duration (e.g., medium-range (MR) tankers, and Caribbean and Latin America trade loops for containerships). While voyage days are generalized due to route variability, they provide a baseline for estimating cumulative CO₂ generation per arrival - a prerequisite for sizing shore-based reception systems. Engine sizes and visit frequencies are derived from the port’s public statistics information and cargo priorities, particularly phosphate exports and distillate imports dominating bulk and tanker traffic. The projections hinge on several key assumptions requiring consideration: A 10% adoption rate of onboard carbon capture systems (OCCS) is estimated, reflecting a conservative scenario where regulatory incentives or global emission fees drive early adoption. In practice, actual participation could fall below 5% due to high retrofit costs, operational complexities, or slow regulatory mandates, or surge beyond 20% if carbon pricing mechanisms or stringent emission regulations are implemented. Another key assumption is the 25% capture rate which assumes amine scrubbers achieve baseline efficiency under ideal conditions, though real-world performance may vary by ±10% due to OCCS performance metrics, renewable fuels availability, or system downtime. Voyage days and fuel consumption are derived from industry averages, but individual vessel routing (e.g., shorter Gulf Coast shuttles vs. transatlantic hauls) and speed optimization practices could alter actual CO₂ generation by 15–30%.
